modules.name: Arithmetic
modules.header:
Checked, wrapping and saturating integer arithmetic, at every integer width the language spells.
Each operation is generic over the integer type rather than repeated per width. Nothing here needs to be told which
type it has: an integer's zero, its all-ones pattern, its signedness and its two limits all follow from one operand
and the wrapping arithmetic the machine already does, so `int8` and `uint512` run the same code. Every helper below
derives what it needs the same way:
  zero     = value - value           the type's zero
  allOnes  = zero - 1                every bit set: the maximum when unsigned, -1 when signed
  signed   = allOnes < zero          only a signed type reads all-ones as negative
  signBit  = 1 << (sizeof(T) * 8 - 1)  the top bit, which is the most negative value when signed
Ordinary `+`, `-` and `*` wrap on overflow, which is what makes the checks below possible: they compute the wrapped
answer and then ask whether it is the true one.
The operation comes first in each name because `CheckedAdd`, `CheckedSub` and `CheckedMul` already name the
compiler's own intrinsics, which are emitted inline for `uint64` and are the ones allocation-size arithmetic is
written with. These are the general family: any integer width, signed or unsigned, at the cost of being ordinary
code rather than an inline sequence.

modules.name: Bits
modules.header:
Bit-level operations on integers, at every integer width the language spells.
Like the arithmetic beside them, these are written once and generic over the integer type rather than repeated per
width, and they derive what they need from one operand: `sizeof(T) * 8` is the width, `value - value` is the type's
zero, and `zero + 1` is its one.
Signedness is the thing to be careful about here, because `>>` is arithmetic on a signed type: it copies the sign
bit down instead of bringing zeros in. Every operation below that has to see a value's bits as bits rather than as
a number goes through `ShiftRightLogical`, which brings zeros in at either signedness. Reading a single bit with
`(value >> index) & 1` needs no such care — whatever arithmetic shift replicated above bit zero is masked away.
Nothing here is a machine instruction. A back end may recognize some of these shapes, but the count and reversal
operations are written as loops over the width so that a 512-bit type behaves exactly like an 8-bit one.

modules.name: Build
modules.header:
What the active build is doing, as ordinary values available while compiling.
`#build` answers questions about the build rather than about the machine it targets, which is `#target`'s job: the
profile chosen, what the profile implies, what artifact is coming out, and when it was made. Reading one costs
nothing at run time, because the value is folded where it is written.
The timestamp is fixed once per build rather than read per expression, so every use of it in one build agrees. That
makes it usable as a build identity and unusable as a clock.

modules.name: Checked
modules.header:
The three arithmetic operations that report overflow instead of producing it.
Compiler intrinsics rather than Rux source, because the answer and the overflow flag come out of one
machine instruction and no expression in the language can name both. Each reports `true` for failure,
which reads backwards the first time and is the convention the whole checked family agrees on.
These take `uint64`. `Core::Arithmetic` is the generic layer above them, and is what ordinary code calls.

modules.name: Comparable
modules.header:
Ordering: which of two values of one type comes first.
One method, returning a three-way `Ordering` rather than a boolean, because two booleans cannot express
equality without being asked twice. A type that can be ordered can be sorted, searched and bounded by
everything in `Rux/Algorithms` without any of it knowing what the type is.

modules.name: Compiler
modules.header:
The compiler performing the build, and the version type it reports itself with.
`#compiler` is what a package uses to require a language feature rather than to guess at one from a version
number, which is what `HasFeature` is for. `SemanticVersion` lives here because the compiler's version is the
first thing that needed one; it is an ordinary value type usable for any version.

modules.name: Config
modules.header:
User-defined build values, read while compiling.
A project sets these in `[Build.Defines]` or on the command line with `--define`, which is how a build carries a
choice that is neither a target property nor a profile property — a feature switch, a vendor name, a limit.
Everything here is answered while compiling and produces no runtime code. A name that was never defined is absent
rather than empty, which `Has` is for: `Get` on an absent name yields an empty value that an intentionally empty
definition also yields.

modules.name: Convert
modules.header:
Conversions between primitive types that report what the cast alone does not: whether the value survived.
`as` always produces a value of the destination type, wrapping or truncating whatever did not fit and saying
nothing about it. That is the right default for the places a conversion is known to be safe, and the wrong one
everywhere else — an index narrowed to a smaller width, a signed count handed to an unsigned parameter, a
measurement rounded to a narrower float. These say what happened.
Every check here is a round trip: convert, convert back, and compare in the source type. Nothing compares a value
of one type against a value of another, so no comparison has to decide which of two widths or signednesses to use.
The round trip catches truncation on its own, and one further test catches the pairs it cannot see — a value and
its conversion that disagree in sign, which is how `-1` reaches `uint64` and how `2^63` reaches `int64` while
converting back to exactly what they started as.
A float source needs no special case. A NaN never equals itself, so the round trip reports it; an infinity converts
back to something finite; and a float narrowed past its precision comes back a different number.

modules.name: Diagnostics
modules.header:
The four ways a program says something is wrong: two that stop it while it runs, and two that stop it being built.
`Assert` and `Panic` report and terminate. Neither unwinds, so no destructor runs on the way out — a program that
panics is not a program whose invariants still hold, and running cleanup code written on the assumption that they do
is how one failure becomes several. Anything that must be released on a failing path has to be released by a caller
that saw the failure, which is what a native fallible `T ! E` is for.
`#Error` and `#Warn` produce no runtime code at all. They are evaluated where they are written, so a configuration
the package does not support is rejected while compiling rather than discovered by whoever runs the result.
All four take their message as a `char8[..]`, the type of an unprefixed string literal.

modules.name: Endian
modules.header:
Byte order: converting an integer between the target's own order and a named one, and moving it to and from bytes.
Two spellings of the same idea are published because they read differently at a call site. `ToLittleEndian` and its
three companions convert a value that is already in a register, which is what a caller writing a header field into
a struct wants. `StoreLittleEndian` and `LoadLittleEndian` move a value through raw bytes, which is what a caller
reading a file or a wire format wants, and they never require the bytes to be aligned for the value's type.
Every conversion asks `TargetIsLittleEndian` which order this machine has, rather than reading `#target.endian`.
The compile-time target is an intrinsic a package brings into scope by importing Core, which Core cannot do for
itself, so the order is established from the target's own storage instead — exactly, and by the one construct that
answers the question without being told: writing a value and reading back the byte it starts with.

modules.name: Equatable
modules.header:
Equality: whether two values of one type stand for the same thing.
Deliberately not derived from `Comparable`: a type can be equatable without being orderable, and forcing
an order on one that has none produces an arbitrary answer that later reads as meaningful.

modules.name: Floating
modules.header:
What a floating-point value is: a number, a zero with a sign, an infinity, or nothing at all.
Every predicate here is arithmetic. None reads the value's bits, which is what lets one implementation serve every
float width the language spells, including the ones lowered in software, whose storage carries padding no generic
function could locate a sign bit inside of. The identities they rest on are IEEE's own:
  value != value              only a NaN is unequal to itself
  value == value - value      only a zero is its own difference; a NaN and an infinity both give a NaN
  value == value + value      only a zero and an infinity double to themselves
  1 / value < 0               a zero's sign, which comparison cannot see, is the sign of the infinity it divides into
Not answered here: whether a finite value is normal or subnormal. Telling those apart needs the format's smallest
normal value, which is a per-width constant rather than something arithmetic recovers, so it belongs with the
per-width constants rather than in a function generic over all of them.

modules.name: Hashable
modules.header:
Hashing: the 64-bit summary a table uses to find a value quickly.
A hash is not an identity. Equal values must hash equally — a table is wrong otherwise — but unequal
values may collide, and a type that implements this must implement `Equatable` consistently with it.
The hasher is supplied by the caller rather than fixed here, so the same type can be hashed by a fast
non-cryptographic function in one table and by a keyed one in another; `Rux/Hash` provides both.

modules.name: Iteration
modules.header:
A cursor that yields a sequence of items one at a time.
The protocol `for` is written against. Nothing here owns a sequence or promises one can be traversed
twice: a cursor is consumed as it goes, and what happens if the sequence changes underneath it is the
sequence's business to document.

modules.name: Ordering
modules.header:
The answer a three-way comparison gives: which side is smaller, or that neither is.
Three cases rather than two booleans, so one comparison answers every question a caller can ask and a
type implementing `Comparable` is asked once rather than twice.

modules.name: Outcome
modules.header:
Which channel a native fallible holds, asked without unwrapping it.
A native fallible `T ! E` is a compiler-owned form with no methods of its own, so the questions every caller asks of
one live here as ordinary generic functions. Each takes the outcome by value, which is what lets a call's result be
asked directly; a named outcome whose payloads cannot be copied is passed as `<-outcome`, and is then gone.
Asking is not handling. A caller that needs the success or the failure matches `.Success(value)` and
`.Failure(error)`, propagates with `?`, or recovers with `catch`; these two are for a branch or an assertion that
needs only the answer.

modules.name: Char
modules.header:
`char`: the canonical character width, which holds a Unicode scalar value.
An alias for `char32`, with identical representation, ABI, constants, conversions and overload identity. It exists so

modules.name: Char128
modules.header:
char128 is a reserved primitive type. Its representation and primitive
constants are not implemented yet.

modules.name: Char16
modules.header:
`char16`: one UTF-16 code unit.
A code unit, not a character: every value that fits is valid, including a surrogate, which is exactly what a code
unit is. A scalar value outside the basic plane takes two of these.

modules.name: Char256
modules.header:
char256 is a reserved primitive type. Its representation and primitive
constants are not implemented yet.

modules.name: Char32
modules.header:
`char32`: one Unicode scalar value.
A scalar value rather than a code unit, so it stops at U+10FFFF and rejects the surrogate range whatever room the
width has beyond it. This is the width `char` names.

modules.name: Char512
modules.header:
char512 is a reserved primitive type. Its representation and primitive
constants are not implemented yet.

modules.name: Char64
modules.header:
`char64`: one Unicode scalar value, in eight bytes.
The same repertoire `char32` holds, in twice the storage: the range stops at U+10FFFF and the surrogates are
rejected, because a scalar value is what this carries. There is no `c64` literal prefix.

modules.name: Char8
modules.header:
`char8`: one UTF-8 code unit.
A code unit, not a character: every value that fits is valid, and a scalar value above U+007F takes more than one of
these. It does not widen implicitly to `char16` or `char32`, because a UTF-8 byte above 0x7F is not the unit of the
same number in either encoding.

modules.name: Int
modules.header:
`int`: a signed integer the width of a pointer on the target.
Sixty-four bits on every currently supported target, and one of the two integer types whose width follows the target
rather than its name. A value that must keep its width across targets should name one that says it.

modules.name: Int128
modules.header:
`int128`: a signed integer in 128 bits, two's complement.
The range is asymmetric, as it is at every signed width: the most negative value has no positive counterpart, which
is behind nearly every edge case in checked arithmetic.

modules.name: Int16
modules.header:

Sixty-four bits on every currently supported target. This is the type a length, an index and a size are spelled in.

modules.name: Uint128
modules.header:

Wrapping is defined at this width and `Min` is zero, so a subtraction that would go below it wraps rather than

modules.name: Source
modules.header:
Where the reading expression is written, as ordinary values available while compiling.
`#source` is not one value: each field is filled in from the place it is read, so passing `#source.line` to a
function reports the caller's line rather than the function's. That is what makes it usable for a logging or
assertion helper, which wants to name the site that called it.

modules.name: Target
modules.header:
The machine being compiled for, as ordinary values available while compiling.
`#target` answers questions about the target rather than about the host running the compiler, which is what makes a
cross-build produce the right code: a package selecting a syscall or a struct layout branches on these and never on
where it happens to be built.
Each variant names one system rather than a family, so the BSDs are told apart. A `when` on one of these keeps only
the branch that applies, so the untaken side is never resolved and may name declarations this target does not have.

modules.name: Zeroize
modules.header:
Clearing storage so that it stays cleared.
Erasing a secret is a write nothing reads back, which is exactly the write dead-store elimination is
entitled to delete, and ordinary source cannot say "and mean it". So this is a compiler intrinsic: the
guarantee is the compiler's rather than a library's, and there is no way to write it otherwise.
It clears the storage it is given and nothing else. A copy made earlier, a value the compiler spilled, or
bytes a reallocation left behind are all still there.

doc.summary: Adds two integers and reports whether the true sum is representable.
doc.markdown:
Adds two integers and reports whether the true sum is representable.
`left` and `right` are read by value. `result` receives the sum the machine produced, which is the true sum when
this returns `false` and the wrapped one when it returns `true`; it is written in both cases, so a caller that
wants the wrapped answer does not have to compute it again. `result` must not be null.
Returns `true` when the sum overflowed. Never traps, so the caller decides what a sum too large to express means.
Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

doc.summary: Shifts an integer right, bringing zeros in at the top whatever its signedness.
doc.markdown:
Shifts an integer right, bringing zeros in at the top whatever its signedness.

doc.summary: Equality: whether two values of one type stand for the same thing.
doc.markdown:
Equality: whether two values of one type stand for the same thing.
The bound a generic writes when it needs to compare its element type — a search, a deduplication, a hash table's
key. `Self` in the signature is the implementing type, so an `Equatable` value is only ever compared against
another of its own type and never against an unrelated one.
An implementation must be an equivalence: a value equals itself, equality reads the same in either order, and two
values each equal to a third are equal to each other. A type that cannot promise all three — one with a value that
does not equal itself, the way a floating-point NaN does not — should not implement this, and callers relying on
it are entitled to assume it holds.
A type that also implements `Hashable` must keep the two agreeable: equal values hash the same.

doc.summary: Hashing: the 64-bit summary a table uses to find a value quickly.
doc.markdown:
Hashing: the 64-bit summary a table uses to find a value quickly.
The bound a generic writes when it keys a hash table or a set on its element type.
The one rule an implementation must keep is agreement with equality: two values that are equal must hash the same.
The converse is not required, and unequal values sharing a hash is an ordinary collision rather than a fault.
Hashing the same value twice in one program run must give the same answer, so an implementation must read only the
value itself — not an address, not a counter, not the clock.
A hash is not a checksum and not a digest: it is not stable across program runs, across compiler versions, or
across targets, and nothing that outlives the process should be keyed on one. `Rux/Hash` supplies the named,
documented algorithms for that, and `Rux/Crypto` the ones that must resist an adversary.

doc.summary: A cursor that yields a sequence of items one at a time.
doc.markdown:
A cursor that yields a sequence of items one at a time.
The compiler drives iteration by shape rather than through this interface: a `for` loop accepts any type with a
`func Next(self: &var Self) -> Item?`, which advances the cursor and reports either the next item or, with `none`,
that the sequence has ended. The item type is whatever that optional carries, and it differs per iterator, so the
method cannot be written here — an interface has no way to name a type its implementor chooses.
What this interface adds is the name. `extend MyCursor : Iterator` records that a type means to be an iterator
and documents which of its methods carry the protocol, and a bound written `<T: Iterator>` says what a generic
expects of its argument. Neither is required to iterate, and a bound on it grants no operations, so a generic that
needs to advance a cursor itself should take the concrete iterator type.
An iterator is consumed as it is read: `Next` mutates it, and an iterator that has reported `none` keeps
reporting `none`. Nothing here promises an iterator can be restarted or copied.
An iterator borrows whatever it walks over. Modifying that container while an iterator over it is alive — growing
a vector, rehashing a map, freeing the storage — leaves the iterator pointing at storage that has moved or gone,
and reading it afterwards is undefined. Finish with the iterator before touching the container.

doc.summary: A value that can hand out an `Iterator` over its contents.
doc.markdown:
A value that can hand out an `Iterator` over its contents.
As with `Iterator`, the compiler matches this by shape: a `for` loop accepts any type with a `func Iterate()` that
returns an iterator, and calls it once at the top of the loop. The returned type differs per container, so the
method cannot be written here either.
`extend MyContainer : Iterable` records the intent and names the protocol; iterating does not require it. Arrays,
slices and ranges are iterated directly by the compiler and implement nothing.
The iterator handed out borrows the container, so the container must outlive it and must not be modified while it
is alive. See `Iterator`.

doc.summary: The answer a three-way comparison gives: which side is smaller, or that neither is.
doc.markdown:
The answer a three-way comparison gives: which side is smaller, or that neither is.
The discriminants are `-1`, `0` and `1` stored in an `int8`, so an ordering costs one byte and its sign is the
comparison's sign. A comparison that cannot decide has no representation here: every pair a comparison is asked
about must land on exactly one of these three.
`Ordering` is a `Copy` value, so reading one never consumes it.

items.name: Zeroize
items.signature: pub func Zeroize(memory: *var uint8, length: uint64)

doc.summary: Overwrites a byte range with zeros, and is never removed however unread those bytes are afterwards.
doc.markdown:
Overwrites a byte range with zeros, and is never removed however unread those bytes are afterwards.
`memory` is borrowed for the call and must address at least `length` writable bytes; passing fewer, or a null
pointer with a non-zero length, is undefined. `length` of zero writes nothing. Nothing is returned.
Clearing a secret is a write nothing reads back, which is exactly what dead-store elimination is entitled to delete.
Ordinary source cannot say "and mean it", so this is a compiler guarantee rather than a library one: every write the
call lowers to is marked as one that must happen.
Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing. It clears the storage it is given and nothing else --
a value copied elsewhere beforehand, or spilled to a register or the stack by the caller, is not reached.
